abstract_text:
SCN1A, encoding the voltage-gated sodium channel (VGSC) Nav1.1, is a major target in neurological disease.
Monoallelic SCN1A variants that result in Nav1.1 haploinsufficiency cause the Developmental and Epileptic
Encephalopathy (DEE) Dravet syndrome (DS) or the less severe Genetic Epilepsy with Febrile Seizures plus
(GEFS+). Gain-of-function SCN1A variants are linked to a more severe, early infantile DEE as well as to Familial
Hemiplegic Migraine Type 3 (FHM3). Despite the importance of SCN1A in the regulation of neuronal excitability,
very little is known about the cell biology of Nav1.1, largely due to the dearth of reliable probes to specifically
localize Nav1.1 channels against the background of other VGSCs in brain neurons at high resolution. Important
questions remain in VGSC cell biology. For example, during brain development, the majority (70%) of newly
synthesized VGSC a subunits enter a metabolically stable intracellular pool while the minority (30%) covalently
associate with VGSC b2 subunits and insert into the plasma membrane. It was proposed that intracellular pools
of newly synthesized a subunits are localized at axon initial segment (AIS) domains and nodes of Ranvier, but
this hypothesis was not tested due to lack of appropriate tools. The existence of a large pool of newly synthesized
VGSC a subunits in neurons raises important questions about why haploinsufficiency matters in pediatric
neurological disease. Our work has demonstrated that treatment of DS mice with the TANGO antisense
oligonucleotide STK-001 corrects Nav1.1 haploinsufficiency and sodium current density as well as restores
neuronal excitability. Administration of STK-001 to wildtype mice also increases Nav1.1 expression and sodium
current density but does not alter the firing properties of interneurons or result in toxicity. Why not? Where are
these newly synthesized VGSCs located in neurons? Finally, the specific composition of the “channelome” is
critical for the regulation of neuronal excitability, e.g. a particular VGSC a subunit subtype located at the AIS may
function differently than the same a subunit located at dendrites due to the differential cohort of modulatory
proteins with which the channel associates in these subcellular domains. Future work requires high resolution
imaging of Nav1.1 and proteomic identification of Nav1.1 interacting proteins at specific subcellular neuronal
domains. A critical unmet need in VGSC biology is the availability of reliable mouse models expressing epitope-
tagged VGSC subunits. We have successfully generated transgenic mouse models expressing epitope-tagged
Nav1.2 and b1 subunits, respectively, but a tagged Nav1.1 model is not currently available. Thus, this R03
proposal contains a single aim: To generate and validate an epitope-tagged Nav1.1 transgenic mouse line
that can be made widely available to the VGSC field through deposition in the Jackson Laboratories
Repository. This novel mouse strain will be invaluable to researchers studying DS, GEFS+, and FHM3.
project_title: Development of an epitope-tagged Nav1.1 transgenic mouse model
phr_text:
SCN1A, encoding the voltage-gated sodium channel (VGSC) Nav1.1, is a major target in neurological disease.
A critical unmet need in VGSC biology is the availability of reliable mouse models expressing epitope-tagged
VGSC subunits. The goal of this R03 proposal is to generate and validate an epitope-tagged Nav1.1 transgenic
mouse line that can be made widely available to the VGSC field through deposition in the Jackson Laboratories
Repository.
